title: The free uniform spanning forest
author: Claude Opus 5.5 (Anthropic)
description: A spanning tree of a finite connected graph, chosen with probability proportional to the product of weights on its edges. The first lesson proves the matrix-tree theorem with the formula of Cauchy and Binet, the expressions of the inclusion probabilities and covariances of edges through the inverse of the reduced Laplacian, the fact that different edges are never positively correlated, and the response identity: the absolute values of the derivatives of the inclusion probability of an edge with respect to the logarithms of all weights add up to 2p(1 - p), at most one half, for every graph and all weights. The second lesson constructs the free uniform spanning forest of an infinite connected graph in which every vertex lies on finitely many edges: the probability that a set of edges lies in the uniform spanning tree of a finite graph is a principal minor of the orthogonal projection onto the complement of the space of circulations; along an exhaustion by finite connected subgraphs these projections converge, and the laws of the uniform spanning trees converge to a probability measure that does not depend on the exhaustion, has no cycles and is carried along by isomorphisms of graphs. The third lesson studies the tilts of the forest by numbers on finitely many edges: a tilt is the conditional law given Gaussian observations of these edges; by the response identity the probability of an edge under a tilt changes by at most half the largest change of the numbers; the drift of an edge, the upper limit of these probabilities along the neighbourhoods of the edge, is a Borel function of all the numbers on the graph that satisfies the same bound and respects isomorphisms of graphs. These are the objects with which OpenAI's proof (2026) shows that this forest is a factor of independent labels; that proof is not yet in the course.
prerequisites: core course Linear Algebra (B40): determinants, expansion along a row, inverse matrices, symmetric matrices
core course Functional Analysis (D20): the Hilbert space of square-summable sequences, orthogonal projections onto closed subspaces

core course Measure and Integration (D10): Lebesgue measure, image measures, product measures and densities, measurable functions and their upper limits, uniqueness of a measure from its values on a generating family closed under intersections
the lessons prove every other fact they use

checks.reading: Lesson 1 was written on 12 Oct 2026 against the lemma 'Weighted-tree response' in Section 2 of OpenAI's manuscript 'The free uniform spanning forest is a factor of IID' (25 Sep 2026); the introduction and Section 2 were read in full, Sections 3 to 6 not yet. Every step was derived; the lesson proves the Cauchy-Binet formula and the rank-one determinant formula, which the manuscript uses without proof. The identities (det L = Z, p_e = c_e a_e^T L^-1 a_e, Cov = -c_e c_f (a_e^T L^-1 a_f)^2, the row sum 2p(1 - p)) were checked in exact rational arithmetic on 40 random weighted connected graphs with up to 6 vertices. No discrepancy with the manuscript. Lesson 2 was written on 12 Oct 2026 against the proposition 'Free exhaustion limit' in Section 2 of the manuscript. Every step was derived; the lesson adds the proofs of det(I + UV) = det(I + VU) and of the fact that a symmetric idempotent matrix is an orthogonal projection, the existence of exhaustions, and two examples. Before the lesson was written, the formula P(F in T) = det (K_H)_F was checked in exact rational arithmetic for 2,051 sets of edges on 25 random connected graphs, together with the symmetry, idempotence and trace of K_H. No discrepancy with the manuscript. Lesson 3 was written on 12 Oct 2026 against the part 'Finite tilts and the canonical drift' of Section 2 and the first step of the lemma 'Posterior drift' in Section 3; Sections 3 and 4 of the manuscript were read in full on that day. Every step was derived; the lesson adds the statement and proof that a tilt is the conditional law given Gaussian observations at one time on finitely many coordinates, the proof that the neighbourhoods of an edge form an exhaustion, and four exercises. Checked numerically before staging (plan/checks_20261012/fu_check_tilts.py): the density identity; the response bound in 8,078 cases on 60 random graphs (largest ratio 0.85 of the bound); derivative equals covariance and the row sums of absolute covariances are at most 1/2 (largest 0.4988); the example with three equal coordinates; the formula for the triangle with three paths. No discrepancy with the manuscript.
checks.layout: Measured on 12 Oct 2026 in the staged pages at widths 1100, 768, 543 and 375 px: lesson 3 has 360 formulas, lesson 2 has 381, lesson 1 has 296; none wider than its column, no formula errors, no horizontal page scroll.

open_obligations: Not yet in the course: the deterministic inversion of the drift (Section 4 of the manuscript, first lemma), which needs only the Lebesgue integral and measurability on spaces of continuous paths.

The main theorem of the manuscript (one Borel equivariant rule that produces the free uniform spanning forest from independent vertex labels on every infinite connected locally finite graph) is not stated or proved in the course. Its proof needs foundations that the programme does not have: Brownian motion and countable families of independent Brownian motions; conditional laws and the filtering of a signal observed in white noise (posterior as an exponential tilt, innovations); the Borel structure on marked graphs and factors of IID; for the last section, strongly Rayleigh measures. See plan/OPENAI_231_SCOPING_20261012.md.
free_sources: OpenAI, The free uniform spanning forest is a factor of IID (OpenAI Math Release preprint, 25 Sep 2026), Sections 1 to 3
